title: Genre & Discourse Awareness

pts: A genre is a recognisable text type — a complaint email, a news report, a personal narrative — with a conventional structure serving a social purpose.
Genres carry expectations that experienced readers or listeners bring to a text before they've read a word of it.
Teaching genre structure explicitly gives learners access to those expectations, not just to vocabulary and grammar.

v: Five short text openings on slips

items: Give pairs five opening lines from different genres (see model language).
Pairs write the genre, the likely reader and the purpose of each.
Pairs predict what comes next in two of the texts.
Discuss: how did you know after only one line?
Build a class chart: genre – purpose – reader – typical opening.
Learners bring openings from home-language texts, translate them, and the class guesses.
Support: a list of genre names to choose from.
Challenge: rewrite one opening so that it signals a different genre.

lines: Once upon a time, in a village near the Kaveri, there lived a potter.
Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing to complain about the delay in delivering my order.
Heavy rain lashed coastal Karnataka on Monday, disrupting train services.
Mix two cups of rice flour with a pinch of salt.
All students of Classes 8–10 are informed that sports day will be held on…

blocks.x: The speed of recognition is the point: readers bring expectations to a text before reading it.

body: Purpose: to show that genre is recognized from small signals. Content: five torn slips, each showing only a first line, with an icon beside each (storybook, envelope, newspaper, cooking pot, noticeboard). Style: clean, playful. Board version: five lines, each with a quick symbol.

items: Wordwall (free basic version) for matching openings with genres.

blocks.x: Slips of paper passed along the benches.

pts: Genres can be broken into predictable 'moves' — a cover letter typically opens with the position applied for, then relevant experience, then a closing request.
Making these moves explicit turns an intuitive native-speaker pattern into an explicitly teachable structure.
This is the analytical technique behind most modern genre-based writing pedagogy.
points.who: John Swales's genre analysis and move structure

v: A short model cover letter; coloured pencils

items: Explain that a move is a stage that does one job for the reader.
Learners colour each part of the letter by its job: position, relevant experience, closing request.
Pairs label each move in their own words.
Compare with a second letter: same moves? Same order?
For teachers: analyse the moves in a circular or government order from your own workplace.
Support: provide the move labels to match.
Challenge: find optional moves that appear in only one letter.

blocks.x: A model letter (written for this book):

lines: [Position] I am writing to apply for the post of junior library assistant advertised on the college notice board.
[Relevant experience] For two years I have helped to organize our class library, cataloguing over three hundred books in English and Kannada.
[Closing request] I would be grateful for the opportunity to discuss my application.

blocks.x: Move analysis turns a pattern that experienced writers use without thinking into something teachable (Swales 1990).

body: Purpose: to show moves as functional stages. Content: a short letter with three shaded blocks, each labelled in the margin (‘Say what you want’, ‘Show why you fit’, ‘Ask for the next step’). Style: clean, textbook-like. Board version: three stacked boxes in coloured chalk.

items: Google Docs (free) highlighter, so pairs can mark moves on a shared copy.

blocks.x: Coloured pencils on a hand-copied letter.

body: Bhatia (1993) analysed job application letters written in South Asia and found moves, such as appeals to the reader’s sympathy, that are less common in letters for British or American readers. [VERIFY exact move labels in Bhatia 1993] Moves reflect communities, not only texts.

pts: Pronouns, connectors, and ellipsis link individual sentences into a coherent, connected text.
This extends Unit 27's discourse competence into concrete, teachable devices learners can apply directly.
Explicit practice noticing these devices in model texts builds awareness faster than incidental exposure alone.

v: A short paragraph with pronouns, connectors and ellipsis

items: Learners circle each pronoun and draw an arrow to what it refers to.
They underline connectors and say what each does: add, contrast, give a reason, show time.
Point out one example of ellipsis: what is missing, and how do we still understand?
Learners rewrite a ‘choppy’ version of the paragraph using the devices they found.
Remove the connectors from a page of the class graded reader (Unit 31); learners restore them.
Support: pronouns only.
Challenge: find lexical cohesion, such as synonyms and repeated words.

lines: Meena wanted to join the school band, but her father was not sure. He thought it would take time from her studies. She promised to practise only at weekends, and he finally agreed. Her brother wanted to join too, but couldn’t.

blocks.x: Reference: her, he, she, it. Conjunction: but, and, finally. Ellipsis: couldn’t [join the band]. A choppy version for rewriting:

lines: Meena wanted to join the school band. Meena’s father was not sure. Meena’s father thought the band would take time from Meena’s studies.

blocks.x: Kannada, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu often drop subjects where English needs a pronoun; a brief comparison helps.

body: Purpose: to show cohesion as visible links. Content: four sentence strips with coloured threads joining each pronoun to its referent and each connector to the sentences it links. Style: diagrammatic. Board version: sentences with chalk arrows.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a printable worksheet.

blocks.x: Arrows drawn by hand on a board text.

pts: Spoken genres — a phone complaint, a job interview, small talk — have their own conventional structures, just as written ones do.
Teaching the typical stages of a spoken genre gives learners a structural map for otherwise unpredictable interaction.
This connects directly to Unit 38's later work on role-play and simulation.

v: A short phone complaint, recorded or read aloud

items: Ask: what happens, step by step, when you phone a shop to complain?
Learners listen to a complaint call (see model language).
Pairs order stage cards: greeting, identify self, state problem, give details, request, agree next step, close.
Learners note one useful phrase per stage.
Pairs perform the call, then swap roles.
Map a job interview, or the same call in a home language.
Support: phrases printed on the stage cards.
Challenge: the caller handles an unexpected reply (We have no record of your order.).

blocks.x: A phone complaint (written for this book):

lines: A: Good morning, Sharma Electronics. How can I help you?
B: Good morning. My name is Arjun Rao. I bought a mixer from your shop last week.
A: Yes, sir.
B: It stopped working after two days. Could you replace it, please?
A: I’m sorry to hear that. Please bring it in with the bill tomorrow.
B: Thank you. I’ll come in the morning. Goodbye.

blocks.x: Spoken genres are less fixed than written ones but still have typical stages (Eggins and Slade 1997; Thornbury and Slade 2006). A map gives learners a structure for unpredictable talk. Unit 38 develops this through role-play and simulation.

body: Purpose: to show a spoken genre as a route. Content: a path of seven stepping stones labelled with the stages, with two speakers holding phones at either end. Style: friendly, map-like. Board version: seven circles joined by a line.

items: Vocaroo (free) for recording and replaying calls.

blocks.x: The teacher reads one role aloud; pairs perform in their seats.

body: Teach one phrase for when the map fails: Sorry, could we go back a step? Learners who know the stages can also notice when a conversation has skipped one.

pts: Analyse authentic model texts for their genre structure before asking learners to produce their own.
This mirrors the guided-discovery principle from Unit 6, applied at the level of whole-text structure rather than a single grammar point.
Multiple models of the same genre reveal which structural features are conventional versus merely one writer's choice.

items: Groups read three short reviews of different products.
They list what the reviews share (structure, tense, typical phrases) and what differs.
Class discussion: which features are conventional and which are choices?
Build a class ‘review recipe’ from the conventions.
Learners write a review using the recipe, adding one choice of their own.
Use three notices from the school board or three short news reports.
Support: a table with rows named (opening, good points, problems, recommendation).
Challenge: compare reviews written for different readers.

blocks.x: Conventions found across three reviews (written for this book):

lines: Opening: what the product is and how long the writer has used it.
Evaluation: good points and problems.
Closing: a recommendation (I’d recommend it for…).

blocks.x: Choices found in only one: a joke in the first line; a star rating; a comparison with an older model. This is guided discovery (Unit 6) applied to whole texts. One model invites copying; several reveal the pattern and the room for choice.

body: Purpose: to separate conventions from choices. Content: three review cards overlapping as a Venn diagram; the shared centre lists conventional moves, the outer parts individual choices. Style: clear. Board version: three overlapping circles.

items: Padlet (free plan) with a column per model and one for the recipe.

blocks.x: Three reviews on the board, one per section of the class.

pts: Genre conventions vary across languages and cultures — an effective complaint letter's structure isn't universal.
This connects to Unit 24's intercultural competence work, applied specifically to written and spoken genre structure.
Make L1 genre differences explicit where relevant, rather than assuming a single universal template.

v: A formal letter or invitation in a home language and one in English

items: Learners bring or recall a formal letter, invitation or circular in a home language.
Groups describe its stages in English: how does it open, what comes first, how does it close?
Compare with an English text for a similar purpose.
List similarities and differences without judging either as better.
Compare Indian English conventions (Respected Sir, kindly) with those of other Englishes.
Support: groups discuss in the home language, then report one difference in English.
Challenge: rewrite a short letter for a different audience and explain the changes.

lines: Some formal letters in Indian languages open with respectful greetings before stating the business; many international business letters state the purpose in the first line.
Respected Sir/Madam and kindly are well understood in India but may sound very formal elsewhere.

blocks.x: Kaplan (1966) claimed that paragraph organization differs across cultures. These claims were criticized as oversimplified, and later work is more careful (Connor 1996). The teaching point is modest: writers should know which conventions their reader expects. This extends the intercultural work of Unit 24.

body: Purpose: to show genre conventions as cultural. Content: two letters side by side, one in Kannada script and one in English, each with a route showing the order of stages; the routes reach the same destination by different paths. Style: respectful, balanced. Board version: two columns of numbered stages.

items: Google Docs (free) for side-by-side tables.

pts: A genre-aware writing or speaking task gives the task cycle (Unit 28) a clear structural target, not just a topic.
This raises the authenticity and transferability of task outcomes to real-world genre demands.
Genre awareness and task-based teaching combine naturally rather than competing as separate methodologies.

v: Task instructions; a short model proposal

items: Choose a task topic: improving the school canteen.
Add a genre target: a short proposal to the principal.
In the pre-task, show a model proposal and name its moves.
Groups discuss problems and agree solutions.
In planning, groups draft the proposal following the moves.
At the report stage, the class decides which proposal would most persuade the principal.
In language focus, highlight language for recommending.
Make the genre spoken: a two-minute pitch to the school council.
Support: a move skeleton with sentence starters.
Challenge: add a move answering a likely objection.

blocks.x: A proposal skeleton (written for this book):

lines: We are writing to suggest changes to the school canteen.
At present, the lunch queue is very long, and…
We suggest opening a second counter for…
This would mean that…
We would be grateful if you could consider…

blocks.x: A genre target gives the task cycle of Unit 28 a clear outcome. Instead of ‘talk about the canteen’, learners produce a text they may really need.

body: Purpose: to show how genre sharpens a task. Content: an equation of three cards: a canteen picture (‘topic’) plus a letter outline (‘genre’) equals a proposal pinned to the principal’s noticeboard (‘real outcome’). Style: bright. Board version: three boxes with plus and equals signs.

items: Google Docs (free) for group drafting and teacher comments.

blocks.x: Chart paper for each group’s proposal.

pts: A writing or speaking rubric should assess whether the genre's expected structure and moves are present, not just sentence-level grammar.
This previews Unit 46's rubric-design work, applied specifically to genre and discourse competence.
Genre awareness gives concrete, teachable criteria for what otherwise risks being vague feedback like 'organise it better.'

items: Choose a genre you assess, and list its expected moves and cohesive features.
Draft rubric rows for purpose and audience, moves, cohesion and accuracy.
Write descriptors for three levels in each row.
Score three scripts with a colleague and compare judgements.
Revise descriptors you disagreed on.
Turn the rubric into a learner checklist for self- and peer-review (Unit 43).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One row for a complaint email (written for this book):

lines: Moves – 3: states the problem, gives details, makes a clear request, closes politely. 2: most moves present; request unclear. 1: no request; stages out of order.
Organize it better.
You explained the problem well, but you never said what you want the company to do. Add a request before your closing line.

blocks.x: The second can be acted on because it names a move. Unit 46 develops rubric design more fully.

body: Purpose: to show assessment above the sentence. Content: a learner’s letter with small corrections in the text and larger margin notes on moves (‘Request missing’, ‘Good opening’). Style: realistic. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free) comments for move-level feedback.

blocks.x: A printed rubric stapled to each script.

body: With the next set of letters you mark, write one comment on each script about a move before correcting any grammar: one move that is strong and one that is missing or weak. Notice whether the next pieces change.

dek: Unit 33 of 100: real texts belong to genres with predictable structures — recognising them helps learners navigate and produce whole texts, not just correct sentences.

aims.x: This unit moves attention above the sentence. It shows how real texts, written and spoken, belong to genres with recognizable purposes and stages, and how making those stages visible helps learners handle whole texts. It builds on the discourse competence of Unit 27 and prepares for genre-based writing in Unit 54.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain what a genre is and why its structure follows from its purpose;
carry out a simple move analysis of a short text;
teach learners to notice and use reference, ellipsis and connectors;
map the stages of a spoken genre;
use several model texts to separate conventions from one writer’s choices;
discuss genre differences across languages without treating one as correct;
give a task a genre target and assess it with genre-aware criteria.

why: Why this matters. A learner can write grammatically correct sentences that still fail as an email, a report, or a story, because genre structure operates above the sentence level.

background.x: A learner can write twelve correct sentences and still fail to write a good complaint email. What is missing is knowledge of the genre: a recognizable type of text that a community uses to get something done. John Swales (1990) defined genres as communicative events whose members share communicative purposes, and showed that those purposes shape structure. His analysis of research article introductions as a sequence of moves became a model for describing many genres; Vijay Bhatia (1993) extended it to professional texts such as sales letters and job applications.

A second tradition, the Sydney School of J. R. Martin and David Rose, developed a teaching–learning cycle in which teachers deconstruct a model text, construct a new one jointly with the class, and only then ask learners to write alone (Martin and Rose 2008). Ken Hyland (2004, 2007) argues that genre pedagogy makes the expectations of powerful texts explicit, giving access to learners who do not already carry them from home. Below structure lies cohesion: the ties that link sentences, described by Halliday and Hasan (1976) as reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical cohesion. Cohesion is not coherence, but noticing it helps learners read and write connected text.

Genre work suits Indian classrooms. Board examinations already reward genres such as the formal letter, the notice and the report, though these are often memorized as fixed formats. The NCF 2023 asks for language use for varied purposes in real contexts (NCERT 2023), and NEP 2020 encourages home languages as a resource (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). Learners already know many genres in Kannada, Hindi, Tamil or Urdu: the wedding invitation, the cricket commentary, the family WhatsApp greeting. Those genres are a bridge to English, and comparing them is itself genre awareness.

items: Move check. Learners mark the moves in a new text of a familiar genre.
Cohesion task. A short text with gaps for pronouns and connectors, completed and explained.
Genre production. A short written or spoken text scored with the genre-aware rubric.
Genre comparison. A short reflection comparing an English genre with a home-language one.
Which genres do your learners need now, and which after school?
Do you teach formal letters as fixed formats or as texts with purposes?
How many model texts do learners see before they write?
Does your feedback mention structure, or mostly grammar?

terms.def: The quality that makes a text make sense as a whole, with logically connected and relevant ideas; coherence depends on meaning, whereas cohesion depends on visible links.
The linking of sentences and ideas in a text through visible language devices such as pronouns, conjunctions, repetition and synonyms.
The omission of words that can be understood from context, as in ‘You free?’ for ‘Are you free?’ It is common in conversation and a key feature of spoken grammar.
A type of text with a recognized social purpose and typical stages and language, such as a recount, a complaint letter, a lab report or a nursing handover.
An assessment rubric whose criteria reflect the purpose, stages and language of a particular genre, rather than generic features that apply to any text.
The study of how writing conventions differ across cultures and how writers negotiate them, without assuming that one culture’s patterns are superior (Connor 2011).
In genre analysis, a stage of a text that performs a recognizable communicative function, such as ‘establishing a territory’ at the start of a research article introduction (Swales 1990).
Identifying the sequence of moves in texts of a genre and the language typically used to realize each move (Swales 1990); it gives learners a map for reading and writing that genre.

A cohesive device in which a word such as a pronoun, demonstrative or comparative points to something mentioned elsewhere in the text (Halliday and Hasan 1976). In ‘Ravi lost his bag. He found it later’, he and it are reference items.

A recognizable type of spoken interaction with a social purpose and typical stages, such as storytelling, service encounters or gossip (Eggins and Slade 1997). Mapping its stages gives learners a structure for unpredictable talk.
